about: The player's standing in the valley (T164, ADR 0025): for each virtue, a sum of the fixed weights below over every deed in the record. A designer wrote each weight and its reason; nothing at game time changes one. Two players who did the same deeds have the same standing, however they played. It estimates no skill and sets no difficulty: the only things it may set are the consequences listed here, and T165 gives them their thresholds.

virtues.care: How much the valley believes the player looks after it: what was built, mended and fed, less what was ruined.
virtues.fear: How much the valley is afraid of the player: what was destroyed or cut off, whether or not it was meant as harm.

consequences.price: What a trader asks of the player at the market.
consequences.door: Whether a door in the village opens to the player.
consequences.greeting: What a villager says when the player comes near.

weights.why: The grain burnt with the barn was everybody's bread; whoever burns it is a danger to the whole valley.
Without the mill nobody grinds; it is the same harm as the barn, by another road.
Trees take years to bear again, but nobody goes hungry this winter for it.
Mending the barn gives the valley its bread back; it frightens nobody.
Mending the mill gives the valley its flour back.
A bridge built up again brings the travellers and their trade back.
Cutting the valley off from the road harms the market a little, and shows a strength people fear.
A crossing on foot is work done for everyone who comes to the market.
It waters the field and stops the mill: help to one, harm to another, and the sign of someone who moves rivers.
Sowing a field is ordinary work, and a small kindness.
Planting trees is work for people who will eat the fruit after the planter is gone.
A well is the most generous thing anyone does here: water for every house, for good.
An open gate lets the goats into the orchard: careless rather than cruel.
Shutting the gate behind you is what a good neighbour does.
